content: MeNZB is a vaccine specifically designed to target a particular strain of group B meningococcus. It is currently being utilized in New Zealand to manage an ongoing epidemic of meningococcal disease. While most individuals can carry the meningococcus bacteria without experiencing any adverse effects, the disease itself can lead to severe conditions such as meningitis and septicaemia. These complications can result in brain damage, organ failure, extensive damage to the skin and soft tissues, and even death. The immunization process with MeNZB requires three doses, which are typically administered approximately six weeks apart. However, for newborns, the doses are given alongside their routine vaccinations at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 5 months of age. It is important to note that even individuals who have been fully immunized with MeNZB may still carry the meningococcus bacteria and remain susceptible to contracting meningococcal disease. Each dose of the vaccine is 0.5 ml and contains the following components: 25 micrograms of outer membrane vesicles derived from the Neisseria meningitidis group B strain NZ98/245. 1.65 milligrams of aluminum hydroxide, which serves as an adjuvant. Histidine, which acts as a pH stabilizer. Normal saline, which is a sterile solution of salt and water. The vaccine does not contain any whole bacteria, whether alive or dead. Instead, it includes outer membrane vesicles, which are small fragments of the bacterial outer membrane. These vesicles enable the immune system to recognize and prepare for potential infection by the actual bacteria. Importantly, the vaccine does not contain any human, blood, or bovine-derived products, nor does it include egg products, neomycin, or the preservative thiomersal (mercury). Additionally, there are no live meningococcal bacteria in the vaccine, meaning it is impossible to contract the disease or become a carrier of the bacteria from receiving the vaccine. The immune system typically does not respond to outer membrane vesicles when they are presented alone. To address this, the vaccine includes an adjuvant, aluminum hydroxide, which prevents the breakdown and elimination of the vesicles. The adjuvant also induces localized tissue damage, which helps provoke the desired immune response. The saline solution serves as a medium to dissolve all the components into an injectable form, with a salinity level matching that of normal human body fluids. The antigen in MeNZB is derived from the B:4:P1.7b,4 (NZ98/254) strain of Neisseria meningitidis. The bacteria are cultivated in a fermentor using a synthetic culture medium that contains sugar, essential amino acids, and critical elements such as iron and potassium. No bovine or porcine products are used during the fermentation process. The bacterial outer membranes are extracted using the detergent deoxycholate, which effectively kills the bacteria. The outer membrane vesicles are then purified from the culture medium through ultracentrifugation, stabilized with histidine, and adsorbed onto aluminum hydroxide as an adjuvant. The purification process is further refined using ultrafiltration and diafiltration techniques. Since its introduction, the MeNZB vaccine has had a significant impact on controlling the meningococcal epidemic in New Zealand. The vaccine was originally developed in Norway but was not widely distributed there because the Norwegian epidemic subsided before the vaccine was ready for release. Furthermore, Norwegian health authorities did not approve their version of the vaccine for use in infants and young children.
